newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's SPD seeks tax deal but maintains demands.
newsitem.headline: Germany's SPD seeks tax deal but maintains demands.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Sunday affirmed clear differences with the ruling coalition over the shape of possible tax reforms while asserting their readiness to negotiate in key talks this week.

"There must be a breakthrough at the tax negotiations," said SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine, who will meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday in an attempt to avert a parliamentary battle over Kohl's major tax reform project
But Lafontaine, in a statement, repeated SPD calls for increased child subsidies and a higher minimum for tax-free income than Bonn has proposed.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping also said the opposition was ready to bargain, but opposed Bonn's promise of a net tax reduction of 55 billion marks a year.
"We are more than open to any proposal the coalition makes," Scharping said in an interview with the Bild am Sonntag newspaper. A net cut of 10 billion to 15 billion marks was practical, he said.
Scharping also repeated support for an increase in child subsidies, cuts in job insurance contributions and a private asset tax -- ideas coalition leaders criticised at the weekend.
An increase in benefit payments to families that have children would cost 3.6 billion marks, and could be paid for with a new private asset tax, Scharping said.
"The government scrapped this tax and threw between five and six billion marks out the window," Scharping said.
Cuts in employee and employer contributions to job insurance could be paid for later through reducing government bureaucracy and cutting other subsidies, Scharping said.
The SPD wants to cut these job overheads by July 1 to help ease Germany's near-record unemployment, which fell by 190,000 in March to 4.3 million.

But the July 1 date will be out of reach if Bonn does not agree to the cuts on Tuesday, Lafontaine said, who called for the child subsidy rise and job overhead reductions on Friday in a list of demands for the tax talks.

Wolfgang Gerhardt, the head of Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), said the SPD had been raising new demands as part of an effort to delay tax reforms to discredit the coalition with voters.
It was a "narrow-minded strategy to destroy jobs," he said in Bild am Sonntag.

Kohl's closest aide, Wolfgang Schaeuble, told the newsweekly Der Spiegel the coalition was ready to discuss "all points, all proposals," but had doubts "whether the SPD is serious and wants to cooperate on reform."
Kohl's coalition has sought cuts of 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes over two years in an effort to revive the economy to help meet the criteria for European monetary union.
The SPD quit the tax talks in February in a row over coal subsidies.
If the latest talks fail, the reform battle will move to parliament, where the SPD can block tax measures through its majority in the upper house.
